Lecture 3
Autocorrelation and
Model selection

\[ {\textbf{Autocorrelation Function}} \newcommand{\var}{\text{var}} \newcommand{\cov}{\text{cov}} \newcommand{\cor}{\text{cor}} \]

Autocorrelation

Consider a time series \(Y_t\)

  • Mean: \(E(Y_t)=\mu_t\)
  • Variance: \(\var(Y_t)\).

The autocovariance of \(Y_t\) at lag \(j\) is \[ \cov(Y_t,Y_{t-j}) = E[ \: (Y_t-\mu_t) \, (Y_{t-j}-\mu_{t-j}) \:] \]

Autocorrelation

Consider a time series \(Y_t\)

  • Mean: \(E(Y_t)=\mu_t\)
  • Variance: \(\var(Y_t)\).

The autocorrelation of \(Y_t\) at lag \(j\) is \[ \cor(Y_t, Y_{t-j}) = \frac{\cov(Y_t, Y_{t-j})} {\sqrt{\var(Y_t) \: \var(Y_{t-j})}} \]

Autocorrelations in data

For any \(j\): \[ \widehat\cov(Y_t, Y_{t-j}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=j+1}^n (Y_t-\widehat\mu_t) \ (Y_{t-j}-\widehat\mu_{t-j}) \] where typically \[ \widehat\mu_t = X_t'\widehat\beta \]

Note \(\widehat\var(Y_t) = \widehat\cov(Y_t, Y_{t-j})\) with \(j=0\).

Autocorrelations in data

For any \(j\): \[ \widehat\cov(Y_t, Y_{t-j}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=j+1}^n \widehat{Z}_t \widehat{Z}_{t-j} \qquad\qquad\qquad\:\:\: \] where \(\widehat{Z}_t=Y_t-X_t'\widehat{\beta}\) are residuals from regression on trend, seasonals etc as appropriate.

Autocorrelations in retail sales

Y <- window(log(Retail_q), start=c(2000,1), 
            end=c(2018,4))
Time <- time(Y)
gfc <- 2008.5
Time_postgfc <- 1*(Time>gfc)*(Time-gfc)
QD <- seasonaldummy(Y)
X <- cbind(Time, Time_postgfc, QD)
AR0 <- Arima(Y, order=c(0,0,0), xreg=X)
Z <- AR0$residuals

Autocorrelations in retail sales

Z <- AR0$residuals
acfZ <- acf(Z)
print(round(acfZ$acf[1:5],3))

A formal autocorrelation test

checkresiduals(AR0)

    Ljung-Box test

data:  Residuals from Regression with ARIMA(0,0,0) errors
Q* = 92.465, df = 8, p-value < 2.2e-16

Model df: 0.   Total lags used: 8

A formal autocorrelation test

Ljung-Box test statistic: \[ Q^* = n(n+2)\sum_{k=1}^{\color{lime}{l}} \frac{{\color{orange}{r_k}}^2}{n-k} \]

\(\quad {\color{orange}{r_k}} = \widehat{\cor}(\widehat{Z}_t,\widehat{Z}_{t-k})\)

\(\quad {\color{lime}{l}}=\min(8,n/5)\) for quarterly data.

A formal autocorrelation test

Ljung-Box test statistic: \[ Q^* = n(n+2)\sum_{k=1}^{\color{lime}{l}} \frac{{\color{orange}{r_k}}^2}{n-k} \]

\(\quad H_0: \text{all autocorrelations are zero}\)

\(\quad H_1 : \text{at least one autocorrelation not zero}\)

Reject \(H_0\) for \(p<0.05\), where the \(p\)-value for \(Q^*\) uses a \(\chi_{l-p}^2\) distribution.

A formal autocorrelation test

\({\color{magenta}{\dfrac{}{\quad\quad\: \Rightarrow \: \text{reject } H_0 \:}}}\)

Why does autocorrelation matter?

Recall the one-step-ahead forecast errors \[ U_t = Y_t - E(Y_t | {\mathscr{F}}_{t-1}) \] satisfy \(E(U_t | {\mathscr{F}}_{t-1}) = 0\), and hence \[ \cor(U_t, U_{t-k}) = 0 \text{ for every } k>0 \]

\({\color{orange}{\Rightarrow}}\) if residuals from a model are autocorrelated then that model is misspecified for the conditional expectation.

\[ {\textbf{Model selection}} \newcommand{\var}{\text{var}} \newcommand{\cov}{\text{cov}} \newcommand{\cor}{\text{cor}} \]

Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)

Consider a model \(m(Y_{t-1},Y_{t-2},\ldots; \theta)\) of \(E(Y_t|{\mathscr{F}}_{t-1})\).

Example. AR(p): \[ \begin{align} m(Y_{t-1},&Y_{t-2},\ldots; \theta) \\ = & \theta_1 Y_{t-1} + \ldots + \theta_p Y_{t-p} \end{align} \]

Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)

Consider a model \(m(Y_{t-1},Y_{t-2},\ldots; \theta)\) of \(E(Y_t|{\mathscr{F}}_{t-1})\).

Define residuals \[ \widehat{U}_t = Y_t - m(Y_{t-1},Y_{t-2},\ldots; \widehat\theta) \] and residual variance \[ \hat\sigma_U^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^n \widehat{U}_t^2. \]

Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)

The AIC is \[ \text{AIC} = n \log(\hat\sigma_U^2) + 2 (M+1) \] where \(M\) is the number of parameters in \(\theta\).

Eg. \(M=p\) for the AR(p) model.

Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)

The AIC is \[ \text{AIC} = n \log(\hat\sigma_U^2) + 2 (M+1) \] where \(M\) is the number of parameters in \(\theta\).


Model selection:

Choose a model to make AIC as small as possible.

Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)

The AIC is \[ \text{AIC} = n \log(\hat\sigma_U^2) + 2 (M+1) \] where \(M\) is the number of parameters in \(\theta\).


Small \(\sigma_U^2 \Rightarrow\) Model fits well.

Small \(M \Rightarrow\) Model is parsimonious.

Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)

The AIC is \[ \text{AIC} = n \log(\hat\sigma_U^2) + 2 (M+1) \] where \(M\) is the number of parameters in \(\theta\).


Technically: AIC is an estimate of the “Kullback-Leibler distance” of the model from the true data distribution.

Corrected Akaike Information Criterion

The AICc is \[ \text{AICc} = \text{AIC} + \frac{2M^2+2M}{n-M-1} \]

AICc generally has superior accuracy in smaller samples.

Illustration of model search

We can compute the autocorrelation test and AIC for each model specification combining:

  • X1: linear trend only

  • X2: linear trend and quarterly dummies

  • X3: linear trend, GFC trend break, quarterly dummies

  • AR(p), \(p=0,1,2,\ldots\).

\[ {\textbf{Lecture 3 Summary}} \]

Lecture 3 Summary

  • Autocorrelation function describes autocorrelation properties of time series and residuals.

  • The Ljung-Box autocorrelation test is used to test model residuals

  • The AIC(c) is used to choose amongst forecasting models.
